title: Adding an API Client or AI Agent

blocks.text: Applications, services, and AI agents that need to access Zscaler API resources must be provisioned in the Zscaler Admin Console. When a client requests authorization, Authentication Service validates the request and issues an access token. The API client or AI agent uses this access token to request access to the required API resources.

Authentication Service supports the OAuth Client Credentials and Authorization Code grant types. The Client Credentials grant type enables applications and services to access API resources without user interaction, while the Authorization Code grant type to enable applications and AI agents to access API resources on behalf of authenticated users.
You can manually configure an API client or select a predefined AI client, such as ChatGPT or Claude.

Authentication Service admins assigned with Full permission to access the API Clients and API Resources modules can configure API clients in the Zscaler Admin Console. To learn more, see Admin Roles and Permissions. If your organization uses Unified Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), administrator roles for Authentication Service and some Zscaler services are managed on a different Role Management page. To learn more, see About Role Management. Unified RBAC is a feature in limited availability. To access Unified RBAC, contact your Zscaler Account team.
To add an API client or a predefined AI client:

blocks.item: From the navigation menu, go to Administration > API > API Clients.
See image.
Click Add API Client and select an option (New Client, Claude, or ChatGPT), and configure the API client or AI agent:
New API Client
On the Add API Client page, the Client tab is selected by default. Enter the following details:
In the Client Information section:
Name: Enter a name to identify the API client.
Description: Enter a brief description that indicates the purpose of the API client (e.g., a software application or a script that is using this name to interact with OneAPI).
Status: Enable the status. This allows the API client to authenticate and use the API resources.
When the status is disabled, the API client cannot get the access tokens issued by Authentication Service.

Access Token Validity (in minutes): The validity of the access token that is used to access the API resource. Enter the time in minutes. The minimum and maximum validity periods are 1 minute and 24 hours, respectively.
In the Grant Types section, select one of the following grant types:
Client Credentials: Enables applications and services to access Zscaler APIs without user interaction.

Authorization Code: Enables applications and AI agents to access Zscaler APIs on behalf of authenticated users using the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. If you select Authorization Code, configure the following additional settings:
Redirect URIs: Enter one or more redirect URIs, separated by commas, and click Add. These URIs specify where users are redirected after authorization.
Grant Lifetime (in days): Enter the number of days for which the authorization grant remains valid. The default and maximum duration is 365 days.

In the Client Authentication section, configure any of the following supported authentication methods: JSON Web Key (JWK) specification, certificates and public keys, Secret, or None. You also need to set up the same authentication method in your application. For example, if you configure JWK in the Zscaler Admin Console, your application should sign and verify the JSON Web Token (JWT) with the same key when sent for authentication. To learn more, see Getting Started.

Client JWKs URL: Enter the Client JWK URL where the key must be obtained for verification. JWT is a URL-safe token used to securely transmit data between applications. A JWK URL hosts a set of public keys in JSON format, which is used by the API server to verify the signatures of JWT issued by the API client.
See image.
Certificates/Public Keys: Upload a PEM file that contains the public key. Authentication Service reads the public key and verifies the authentication.
See image.

Secret: Click Add. A key is auto-generated and displayed along with the validity period. This key is generated once, and it cannot be updated. The minimum duration is 30 days and the maximum duration is 365 days. Ensure to copy the secret key and save it in your local folder as it is not going to be displayed again. You can add a maximum of two client secrets. If you add a third one, the new value replaces the most recent client secret. So, at any point in time, there are only two client secrets.
See image.
None: Select this option for public clients that do not use client credentials for authentication. This option is available when you select the Authorization Code grant type.
See image.
On the Resources tab:
You can see the APIs for Zscaler services that are linked to your tenant along with the role (scope). Scope refers to the permission that limits the access to specific API resources.
See image.

Before creating an API client, you must add an API role in the respective Zscaler service (e.g. Internet & SaaS, Private Access). These API roles are synced to Authentication Service and are displayed on the Add API Client page. If you do not configure the API roles, an error message is displayed when you try to assign the resources to the API client. To learn more, see Understanding OneAPI.
Select the required API resources that the API client can access. You can select only one API resource for each Zscaler service and depending on the scope that is assigned.
On the Ownership tab:
Client Owner: Enter the name of the person responsible for the API client.
Client Team: Enter the name of the team responsible for managing the API client.
See image.
Click Save.
If you did not specify a client ID, Authentication Service automatically generates one. The client ID is displayed on the API Clients and AI Agents page.
Copy the client ID and save it, as you need to provide the client ID along with the token or secret to make the API call.
You can also copy the client ID from the Edit API Client drawer:
On the API Clients page, click the Edit icon for the newly configured API client.
In the Edit API Client drawer, copy the client ID and save it in your local folder.
See image.
Predefined AI Agents: Claude or ChatGPT
On the Add API Client page, the Client tab is selected by default. Enter the following details:
In the Client Information section:
Name: Displays the name of the selected AI agent (Claude or ChatGPT). You can modify it as required.
Description: Enter a brief description of the AI agent.
Client ID: Displays the predefined client ID corresponding to the selected AI agent's metadata URL.
Status: Enable this option to allow the AI agent to access API resources.
Access Token Validity (in minutes): Enter the validity of the access token in minutes.
Client Identity Metadata: Enabled by default to retrieve client configuration dynamically from the metadata document.

Grant Types: Displays the grant type retrieved from the client's metadata document. By default, the Authorization Code grant type is selected and it is not editable. If you want to use the Client Credentials grant type, you must disable the Client Identity Metadata option.
Redirect URIs: Displays the redirect URIs retrieved from the metadata document.
Grant Lifetime (in days): Enter the duration for which the authorization grant remains valid. The supported range is 1–365 days, with a default of 365 days.

For predefined AI agents using the Authorization Code grant type, users grant a subset of their assigned administrative permissions during authorization. You do not need to configure API resources or scopes manually.
See image.
On the Ownership tab:
Client Owner: Enter the name of the person responsible for the API client.
Client Team: Enter the name of the team responsible for managing the API client.
See image.
Click Save.
The predefined AI agent is added to the API Clients and AI Agents page.
